From Reader to User

Eighty Years of the Indian Library Association and the Changing Public of the Library, 1942–2019

Working Paper 08 · v0.1.3 · 2026-06

Read the paper (PDF) →

Abstract

This paper reads three sets of primary materials as layered depositions of one history: eighty years of Indian Library Association conference reports (1942–2019), the central government's library-committee reports, and the nineteen state Public Libraries Acts (1948–2009) — the profession, the central state, and the statute book. Across them runs one movement: the disappearance of the reader, the person owed a claim on a reading commons, as one moves from professional speech toward binding law. In the proceedings the reader is renamed the "user," a democratic subject dissolved into a system-function. In the committee reports the reader scarcely appears, and universal provision — costed decade after decade as a right, a cess, a national law — is met each time with deferral. In the Acts, where words bind, the reader is not named at all: the law knows only "the public," "persons," and "members," and the entitlement is hollowed in the statute's own wording — the duty to provide softens to discretion, free access becomes a permitted fee, and the dedicated cess, carried by the early Acts, is dropped by every Act passed after 2000. The recurring answer that libraries are a "State subject" is a political refusal, not a constitutional given. Because the public library matters most to those who cannot buy books — disproportionately the caste-Bahujan poor — and because not one of the nineteen Acts names caste while only Kerala writes representation into its governing bodies, the refusal of universal provision is caste exclusion administered in neutral language.
